one_liner: Short Dyalog APL wc (lines, words, bytes) that ran about 2.9x faster than the stock macOS wc in a 2019 blog test.
what_it_does: A blog-style README plus five variants of a Dyalog APL wc function (src/slow, procfn, windowed, split, mem-split) that return line, word and character counts for a file. You call it from a Dyalog session as wc 'path'; it is not a command-line tool, takes no flags and has no -m/-L modes, so it is not a drop-in replacement for wc.
how_it_is_fast: The file is read in 256 KB blocks with ⎕NREAD, turned into boolean vectors with membership (data∊nl, data∊sp), and counted with whole-array primitives: +/ for newlines and the windowed reduction 2</ to find nonspace-to-space transitions, plus one carry bit (lnsp) to fix words split across blocks. That replaces wc's per-byte scalar loop, which calls the locale-aware iswspace() on every byte, with a few interpreter calls per block over packed booleans. The README gives the windowed version about the same warm time (1.85 s) as a version with word counting removed, so block reading plus membership, not word counting, sets the floor.
when_to_use: You already work in Dyalog APL and need line/word/byte counts of large ASCII text files from inside a session.
Teaching or comparing array-style versus scalar-loop text processing; the README walks from a 32.97 s partition version to the 1.85 s windowed version on the same 1.661 GB file.
Streaming over files larger than memory: the procedural versions and mem-split keep constant memory by reading fixed-size blocks.
As a template for other block-wise boolean-array scans (counting delimiters, field separators) in APL.
when_not_to_use: As a wc replacement: no CLI, no flags, no multibyte character counting, and it needs the proprietary Dyalog interpreter (the author used a free personal copy).
Files with CRLF, CR, VT or FF bytes: bytes 10, 11, 12 and 13 all count as line ends, so CRLF text reports twice wc's line count.
Non-ASCII or locale-dependent text: only six bytes (9-13 and 32) count as whitespace, while wc applies the locale's iswspace(), so word counts can differ.
If you just want a faster wc: catalogued tools such as cw and wz are command-line replacements with flags and hyperfine benchmarks against FreeBSD and GNU wc.
Anything needing maintenance or support: 7 commits, last on 2019-10-26, no issues or releases.

integration.dependencies: Dyalog APL interpreter (proprietary; the README says a free personal copy was used)
integration.min_toolchain: Dyalog APL, version not stated; the slow variant uses the ⊆ partition primitive
integration.platforms: Any platform Dyalog APL runs on; measured only on macOS on a 2.2 GHz Intel Core i7 (early-2015 11-inch MacBook Air)
integration.thread_safety: Not documented; each call ties and unties its own file handle, and the split variant mutates an enclosing variable with ∘←.

gotchas: Harness check: the README never prints the APL output next to wc's, but the test file is Chris Penner's data/big.txt (6,488,666 bytes, pure ASCII, LF line ends, no CR/VT/FF, only space, tab and LF as whitespace) repeated 256 times, which is exactly 1,661,098,496 bytes; on that input both programs' rules give identical counts, so the different line and whitespace definitions do not inflate the measured speedup.

Timing is mixed and unscripted: APL wall time from the dfns timing operator inside a warm session (first runs 3.33-3.36 s, later about 1.85 s) against wc user time from time (5.345-5.549 s); wc system and wall time are not reported, which if anything favours wc. Single file, single machine, no variance, Dyalog version and wc build not stated.

src/split/wc.dyalog and src/mem-split/wc.dyalog contain only the wc dfn; blockCount, blockCollapse or blockAdd and the rc operator they call exist only in the README, so those two variants do not run as checked in.
The words dfn returns 1 for an empty vector (README admits this); the loop never calls it on an empty block, but reusing it elsewhere needs a guard.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Only when you are inside Dyalog APL already: ChrisPenner/wc (the Haskell post this one answers) and hwc make the same point against C wc, while cw and wz are the practical faster wc replacements with flags and hyperfine benchmarks.
verified_claims_summary: On a 1.661 GB file (big.txt x256) on an early-2015 MacBook Air (2.2 GHz Core i7), the windowed-reduction Dyalog APL version took about 1.85 s wall time on warm repeat runs (3.33 s on the first run) while the macOS-shipped C wc took 5.345-5.549 s user time, about 2.9-3.0x (1.6-1.7x on the first run); the first partition-based APL version took 32.97 s. The baseline is a locale-aware scalar wc with unknown build flags, not tuned C.
status_note: Abandoned blog companion (7 commits, last 2019-10-26), BSD-2-Clause and a few dozen lines, so trivially copyable, but it runs only on the proprietary Dyalog interpreter and the evidence stays first-party tier C.
